name: Taking payment with Stripe
summary: Your customers can pay you, and the money arrives in your bank account.

steps.instruction: Create a Stripe account. Use test mode to begin with — you can build everything against it without giving Stripe your bank details.
steps.because: Test mode behaves exactly like the real thing and charges nobody.

steps.instruction: Start Stripe's business verification as soon as you can, even though you cannot take real money yet.
steps.because: Stripe checks who you are before it will pay out to you, and that takes days rather than minutes. Started late, it is the thing that holds up your launch.

steps.instruction: Create a product with a recurring price, and copy its price id.
Copy your test secret key and paste it into the .env file Shipyard made for you.
steps.because: This key can move money. It goes in .env, which stays on your computer and is never sent anywhere.

steps.instruction: Wire the checkout button on the page where the customer decides to pay.
Make one payment with Stripe's test card 4242 4242 4242 4242 and check the subscription appears.
steps.because: Nothing here has moved money. Until one test payment goes through, none of it is proven.

settings.name: STRIPE_PRICE_ID
settings.description: Which plan people are subscribing to.

costNote: Stripe takes a percentage of each payment. There is no monthly fee to start.
limitations: Tax is left to Stripe. Whether that satisfies the rules where you operate is a question for an accountant.
Shipyard never sees your Stripe key, so it cannot tell you the key is valid — only that a payment went through.

name: Stripe telling your app what happened
summary: When a payment succeeds or fails, your app finds out about it.

steps.instruction: In Stripe, add a webhook endpoint pointing at your app's address followed by /api/billing/webhook.
steps.because: Without this your app never learns that a payment succeeded, and a paying customer stays locked out.

steps.instruction: Copy the signing secret it shows you into your .env file.
steps.because: This is what proves a message really came from Stripe. Without it, anyone who finds your address could tell your app they paid.

steps.instruction: Send a test event from the Stripe dashboard and check your app accepted it.

limitations: While you are building on your own computer, Stripe cannot reach your app. Use the Stripe CLI to forward events, or test after your first deployment.

name: Sending email to your users
summary: Your app can email people — sign-in links, receipts, notifications.

steps.instruction: Create an account with an email provider.
Add your domain and put the DNS records it gives you at your domain registrar.
steps.because: Until your domain is verified, your email either does not send or goes straight to spam. DNS changes can take a day to spread, which is why this is worth starting early.

steps.instruction: Copy the API key into your .env file.
Set the address your email comes from. It has to be at the domain you just verified.
Send one real email to yourself and check it arrives in the inbox rather than the spam folder.

settings.name: EMAIL_FROM
settings.description: The address your email comes from.

limitations: Until you set a key, email is printed to the console instead of sent. That is deliberate — it stops a test run emailing real customers.
Whether your email reaches inboxes depends on your domain's reputation, which nothing here can shortcut.

name: Finding out when your app breaks
summary: When something goes wrong for a user, you hear about it instead of guessing.

steps.instruction: Create a free Sentry account and a project for this app.
Copy the DSN it gives you into your .env file.
Open /api/monitoring/test-event in your app once, then check the error appears in Sentry.
steps.because: "We installed error monitoring" and "errors reach us" are different claims. Only the second one is worth anything, and this is the only way to tell them apart.

costNote: The free tier covers a small app comfortably.
limitations: It reports errors your code throws. A page that shows the wrong number without failing is invisible to it.

name: Somewhere to keep uploaded files
summary: People can upload files, and the files are still there tomorrow.

steps.instruction: Create a Cloudflare account and a storage bucket.
Keep the bucket private.
steps.because: Your app hands out short-lived links to the people allowed to see each file. A public bucket makes that pointless — anyone who guesses an address can read anything in it.

steps.instruction: Create an access key with permission to read and write that bucket only.
Copy the key, the secret and the bucket name into your .env file.
Upload one file and download it again.

settings.name: S3_BUCKET
settings.description: The bucket your files go in.

settings.name: S3_ENDPOINT
settings.description: The storage address Cloudflare gives you.

costNote: Cloudflare R2 charges for storage but not for getting files back out, which is the charge that usually surprises people.
limitations: No virus scanning. If strangers can upload, you need that as well.

name: Putting your app on the internet
summary: Your app runs somewhere other than your computer, at an address you can send people.

steps.instruction: Create a Railway account and connect it to your GitHub.
Push the project to a GitHub repository.
Create a project on Railway from that repository.
Copy every setting from your .env into Railway's own variables.
steps.because: Your .env file stays on your computer and is never uploaded. The deployed app has none of those values until you put them there yourself.

steps.instruction: Open the address it gives you and check the app loads.

costNote: Railway charges by usage. A small app costs a few dollars a month.
limitations: Shipyard does not deploy for you and holds no Railway credentials. It can tell you what to do and check the result.

name: A database that lives on the internet
summary: The information in your app is kept somewhere other than your laptop.

steps.instruction: Add a PostgreSQL database to your Railway project.
Copy its connection string into the deployed app's DATABASE_URL variable.
Run the database migrations against it so the tables exist.
Decide how this database gets backed up, and write down the answer.
steps.because: Railway takes backups on some plans and not others. Finding out which after losing data is the expensive way.

limitations: The database Shipyard runs on your computer and this one are separate. Information does not move between them by itself.
